```{r multiple-start-function, include=FALSE}
fit_multiple_starts <- function(response, data, k, seeds) {
  best_fit <- NULL
  best_loglik <- -Inf

  attempts <- data.frame(
    Seed = seeds,
    LogLik = NA_real_,
    Status = NA_character_
  )

  for (i in seq_along(seeds)) {
    set.seed(seeds[i])

    current_fit <- tryCatch({
      model <- depmix(
        response,
        data = data,
        nstates = k,
        family = gaussian()
      )

      fit(
        model,
        verbose = FALSE,
        emcontrol = em.control(
          maxit = 2000,
          tol = 1e-8,
          random.start = TRUE
        )
      )
    }, error = function(e) e)

    if (inherits(current_fit, "error")) {
      attempts$Status[i] <- conditionMessage(current_fit)
      next
    }

    current_loglik <- as.numeric(logLik(current_fit))

    attempts$LogLik[i] <- current_loglik
    attempts$Status[i] <- paste(
      current_fit@message,
      collapse = " "
    )

    if (is.finite(current_loglik) &&
        current_loglik > best_loglik) {
      best_fit <- current_fit
      best_loglik <- current_loglik
    }
  }

  if (is.null(best_fit)) {
    stop("No finite fit obtained for k = ", k)
  }

  best_status <- paste(best_fit@message, collapse = " ")

  if (!grepl(
    "Log likelihood converged to within tol.",
    best_status,
    fixed = TRUE
  )) {
    stop(
      "The highest-likelihood fit for k = ", k,
      " requires a convergence check: ", best_status
    )
  }

  list(
    model = best_fit,
    attempts = attempts
  )
}
```

# Introduction

This analysis investigates whether Gaussian Hidden Markov Models
provide a useful description of Northern Hemisphere temperature
anomalies.

We first estimate models with state-dependent mean levels, both
over the full sample and using observations up to 1975. We then
introduce state-dependent linear trends and compare the resulting
specifications using information criteria and decoded state sequences.

The states are interpreted as statistical summaries of the observed
series, rather than independently established physical climate regimes.

# Data and Seasonal Adjustment

The analysis uses monthly Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies
from GISTEMP, expressed in degrees Celsius relative to calendar-month
means over the 1951–1980 reference period.

We extract the January–December observations and remove a fixed
seasonal component using STL with a periodic seasonal window.
Seasonal adjustment is estimated over the full sample for this
retrospective analysis and re-estimated separately for the sample
ending in 1975.

Since GISTEMP already reports anomalies relative to monthly reference
means, STL removes only residual seasonality. The adjusted series
retains the long-term movement and irregular fluctuations.

```{r load-data}
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "MnGianmaria/time-series-analysis/main/",
  "02_temperature_anomalies_and_forecasting/",
  "data/gistemp.csv"
)

gistemp_raw <- read.csv(
  data_url,
  skip = 1,
  na.strings = "***"
)

month_columns <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)

stopifnot(
  all(month_columns %in% names(gistemp_raw)),
  all(diff(gistemp_raw$Year) == 1)
)

monthly_matrix <- as.matrix(gistemp_raw[, month_columns])
temperature_values <- as.numeric(t(monthly_matrix))

stopifnot(all(is.finite(temperature_values)))

gistemp_ts <- ts(
  temperature_values,
  start = c(gistemp_raw$Year[1], 1),
  frequency = 12
)

seasonal_fit <- stl(
  gistemp_ts,
  s.window = "periodic"
)

temperature_adjusted <- gistemp_ts -
  seasonal_fit$time.series[, "seasonal"]

climate_data <- data.frame(
  Date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(gistemp_ts))),
  Time = as.numeric(time(gistemp_ts)),
  Temperature = as.numeric(temperature_adjusted)
)
```

The sample contains `r nrow(climate_data)` monthly observations,
from `r format(min(climate_data$Date), "%B %Y")` to
`r format(max(climate_data$Date), "%B %Y")`.
The estimated seasonal component ranges from
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(seasonal_fit$time.series[, "seasonal"]))`
to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(seasonal_fit$time.series[, "seasonal"]))`
°C.

```{r adjusted-temperature-plot, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.1, out.width="80%", fig.cap="Seasonally adjusted Northern Hemisphere temperature anomalies. The fixed seasonal component is estimated using periodic STL."}
ggplot(climate_data, aes(x = Date, y = Temperature)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "grey70",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#243746",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
  breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
  date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```

# State-Dependent Level Model

The adjusted series exhibits persistent changes in level.
An HMM provides a way to summarize these patterns through
latent states without fixing transition dates in advance.
Estimated transition probabilities describe persistence and
movement between states. This motivates its use as a
descriptive model, without assuming that the states correspond
to distinct physical climate regimes.

We specify a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model:

\[
Y_t \mid S_t=j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_j,\sigma_j^2),
\]

where \(Y_t\) is the seasonally adjusted temperature anomaly and
\(S_t\) follows a first-order Markov chain with constant transition
probabilities. Observations are assumed conditionally independent
given the state sequence.

Each state has its own mean and standard deviation. We estimate
models with two to five states using the EM algorithm and compare
their AIC and BIC. The model with the lowest BIC is retained within
this candidate set.

Each candidate model is estimated from 25 reproducible random
initializations. We retain the fit with the highest finite
log-likelihood and inspect its convergence status. Multiple starts
reduce sensitivity to initialization but do not guarantee a global
likelihood maximum.

```{r fit-level-models, results='hide', cache=TRUE}
candidate_states <- 2:5
level_seeds <- 123:147

level_runs <- lapply(candidate_states, function(k) {
  fit_multiple_starts(
    response = Temperature ~ 1,
    data = climate_data,
    k = k,
    seeds = level_seeds
  )
})

names(level_runs) <- as.character(candidate_states)

level_models <- lapply(level_runs, function(x) x$model)

level_comparison <- data.frame(
  States = candidate_states,
  LogLik = vapply(
    level_models,
    function(model) as.numeric(logLik(model)),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  AIC = vapply(level_models, AIC, numeric(1)),
  BIC = vapply(level_models, BIC, numeric(1))
)

rownames(level_comparison) <- NULL

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(level_comparison$LogLik)),
  all(is.finite(level_comparison$AIC)),
  all(is.finite(level_comparison$BIC))
)

best_level_k <- level_comparison$States[
  which.min(level_comparison$BIC)
]

best_level_fit <- level_models[[as.character(best_level_k)]]
```

```{r level-model-comparison, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  level_comparison,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("States", "Log-likelihood", "AIC", "BIC"),
  caption = "Comparison of state-dependent level models.",
  table.envir = "table",
  position = "H"
)
```
Both AIC and BIC decrease across the candidate models, reaching their
lowest values with five states. We therefore retain the five-state
specification for further analysis.

Since this is the largest model considered, the comparison does not
establish that five states would remain preferred over a wider candidate
set. Additional states may also approximate a changing temperature
level, rather than identify distinct physical climate regimes.
States are ordered by increasing estimated mean anomaly.
The table reports the Gaussian parameters estimated by the HMM
and the number of observations assigned to each state by Viterbi
decoding. These counts summarize the decoded sequence.

```{r level-state-parameters}
level_parameters <- t(vapply(
  seq_len(best_level_k),
  function(j) {
    getpars(best_level_fit@response[[j]][[1]])
  },
  numeric(2)
))

level_order <- order(level_parameters[, 1])

level_means <- level_parameters[level_order, 1]
level_sds <- level_parameters[level_order, 2]

state_mapping <- integer(best_level_k)
state_mapping[level_order] <- seq_len(best_level_k)

level_states_raw <- posterior(best_level_fit, type = "viterbi")$state
level_states <- state_mapping[level_states_raw]

level_decoded <- climate_data
level_decoded$State <- factor(
  level_states,
  levels = seq_len(best_level_k)
)
level_decoded$StateMean <- level_means[level_states]

level_state_table <- data.frame(
  State = seq_len(best_level_k),
  Mean = level_means,
  SD = level_sds,
  Months = tabulate(level_states, nbins = best_level_k)
)

stopifnot(
  length(level_states) == nrow(climate_data),
  sum(level_state_table$Months) == nrow(climate_data),
  all(is.finite(level_parameters)),
  all(level_sds > 0)
)
```

```{r level-state-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  level_state_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("State", "Mean (°C)", "SD (°C)", "Decoded months"),
  caption = "Estimated state parameters and decoded occupancy.",
  position = "H"
)
```

The decoded sequence is shown below. Colored observations indicate
the most likely joint state sequence, while the black step line
shows the corresponding estimated state mean. Decoding uses the
entire sample and therefore provides a retrospective classification.

```{r level-decoded-plot, fig.cap="Seasonally adjusted temperature anomalies colored by Viterbi-decoded state. States are ordered by increasing estimated mean. The black line follows the estimated mean of the decoded state."}
ggplot(level_decoded, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Temperature),
    color = "grey75",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = Temperature, color = State),
    size = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_step(
    aes(y = StateMean),
    color = "#222222",
    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "#355C7D", "#5A9A9C", "#8A9B55",
      "#D39A45", "#AD5148"
    )[seq_len(best_level_k)]
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```
The estimated state means range from $-0.449\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
to $1.288\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
The earlier observations are mainly assigned to the lower-mean
states, while the two highest-mean states predominantly describe
the later decades.

In the five-state level model, two sustained transitions stand
out in the decoded sequence: entry into State 4 in February 1997,
which persists through November 2014, and entry into State 5
in December 2014, which continues to the sample end.
Before 1980, the path repeatedly switches among lower-mean states.
These dates summarize the fitted retrospective classification;
they are not independently established physical change points.

The decoded path switches repeatedly among the lower states,
whereas the recent warming is represented by sustained higher
levels. This illustrates a limitation of the specification:
a model with constant state means can approximate a gradual
trend through successive changes of state. The decoded transitions
should therefore not automatically be interpreted as abrupt
physical changes in the climate system.

We examine the fitted transition probabilities to assess state
persistence. Each entry gives the probability of moving from
the row state to the column state in the following month.
These are HMM parameter estimates, rather than transition
frequencies calculated from the decoded sequence.

```{r level-transition-matrix}
level_transition_raw <- t(vapply(
  seq_len(best_level_k),
  function(j) {
    as.numeric(
      predict(best_level_fit@transition[[j]])
    )
  },
  numeric(best_level_k)
))

level_transition <- level_transition_raw[
  level_order,
  level_order,
  drop = FALSE
]

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(level_transition)),
  all(level_transition >= -1e-8),
  all(level_transition <= 1 + 1e-8),
  all(abs(rowSums(level_transition) - 1) < 1e-8)
)

level_transition_table <- data.frame(
  From = paste("State", seq_len(best_level_k)),
  level_transition,
  check.names = FALSE
)

names(level_transition_table)[-1] <- paste(
  "State", seq_len(best_level_k)
)
```

```{r level-transition-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  level_transition_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Estimated monthly transition probabilities for the level model.",
  position = "H"
)
```
The estimated probabilities of remaining in the same state range
from approximately 0.900 to 1.000. Transitions mainly occur between
states with adjacent mean levels.

For the highest-mean state, the estimated probability of remaining
in that state rounds to one. The decoded sequence assigns this
state to the final part of the sample, with no observed departure.
This limits the information available about exits from that state;
the estimate should not be interpreted as evidence that the
climate has entered a permanently absorbing regime.

# Analysis up to 1975

We repeat the level-model analysis using observations from January
1880 to December 1975. Periodic STL is re-estimated on this shorter
sample, excluding subsequent observations from seasonal adjustment.

We again compare models with two to five states using AIC and BIC.
These criteria are used to compare specifications within this sample;
their values are not directly comparable with those obtained over
the full sample.

```{r fit-pre1975-models, results='hide', cache=TRUE}
temperature_pre1975 <- window(
  gistemp_ts,
  end = c(1975, 12)
)

seasonal_pre1975 <- stl(
  temperature_pre1975,
  s.window = "periodic"
)

adjusted_pre1975 <- temperature_pre1975 -
  seasonal_pre1975$time.series[, "seasonal"]

climate_pre1975 <- data.frame(
  Date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(temperature_pre1975))),
  Time = as.numeric(time(temperature_pre1975)),
  Temperature = as.numeric(adjusted_pre1975)
)

pre1975_seeds <- 123:147

pre1975_runs <- lapply(candidate_states, function(k) {
  fit_multiple_starts(
    response = Temperature ~ 1,
    data = climate_pre1975,
    k = k,
    seeds = pre1975_seeds
  )
})

names(pre1975_runs) <- as.character(candidate_states)

pre1975_models <- lapply(pre1975_runs, function(x) x$model)

pre1975_comparison <- data.frame(
  States = candidate_states,
  LogLik = vapply(
    pre1975_models,
    function(model) as.numeric(logLik(model)),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  AIC = vapply(pre1975_models, AIC, numeric(1)),
  BIC = vapply(pre1975_models, BIC, numeric(1))
)

rownames(pre1975_comparison) <- NULL

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(climate_pre1975$Temperature)),
  all(is.finite(pre1975_comparison$LogLik)),
  all(is.finite(pre1975_comparison$AIC)),
  all(is.finite(pre1975_comparison$BIC))
)

best_pre1975_k <- pre1975_comparison$States[
  which.min(pre1975_comparison$BIC)
]

best_pre1975_fit <- pre1975_models[[
  as.character(best_pre1975_k)
]]
```

```{r pre1975-model-comparison, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  pre1975_comparison,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("States", "Log-likelihood", "AIC", "BIC"),
  caption = "Comparison of level models for January 1880 to December 1975.",
  position = "H"
)
```
Each candidate model is estimated from 25 reproducible random
initializations. BIC reaches its minimum with three states,
whereas AIC favors the five-state model. We retain three states
according to the stated BIC selection rule. The four-state
specification has a relatively close BIC, differing by
`r sprintf("%.2f", pre1975_comparison$BIC[pre1975_comparison$States == 4] - min(pre1975_comparison$BIC))`
points.

Compared with the five states selected over the full sample,
the shorter period supports a more parsimonious level
representation under BIC. This difference is descriptive:
sample length, seasonal adjustment, and the observed temperature
patterns all change between the two analyses.

States are ordered by increasing estimated mean anomaly.
Their labels refer to this fitted model and do not imply an
exact correspondence with the states of the full-sample model.

```{r pre1975-state-parameters}
pre1975_parameters <- t(vapply(
  seq_len(best_pre1975_k),
  function(j) {
    getpars(best_pre1975_fit@response[[j]][[1]])
  },
  numeric(2)
))

pre1975_order <- order(pre1975_parameters[, 1])
pre1975_means <- pre1975_parameters[pre1975_order, 1]
pre1975_sds <- pre1975_parameters[pre1975_order, 2]

pre1975_mapping <- integer(best_pre1975_k)
pre1975_mapping[pre1975_order] <- seq_len(best_pre1975_k)

pre1975_states_raw <- posterior(best_pre1975_fit, type = "viterbi")$state
pre1975_states <- pre1975_mapping[pre1975_states_raw]

pre1975_decoded <- climate_pre1975
pre1975_decoded$State <- factor(
  pre1975_states,
  levels = seq_len(best_pre1975_k)
)
pre1975_decoded$StateMean <- pre1975_means[pre1975_states]

pre1975_state_table <- data.frame(
  State = seq_len(best_pre1975_k),
  Mean = pre1975_means,
  SD = pre1975_sds,
  Months = tabulate(pre1975_states, nbins = best_pre1975_k)
)

stopifnot(
  length(pre1975_states) == nrow(climate_pre1975),
  sum(pre1975_state_table$Months) == nrow(climate_pre1975),
  all(is.finite(pre1975_parameters)),
  all(pre1975_sds > 0)
)
```

```{r pre1975-state-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  pre1975_state_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("State", "Mean (°C)", "SD (°C)", "Decoded months"),
  caption = "Estimated state parameters and decoded occupancy up to 1975.",
  position = "H"
)
```

```{r pre1975-decoded-plot, fig.cap="Seasonally adjusted temperature anomalies up to December 1975, colored by Viterbi-decoded state. The black line follows the estimated mean of the decoded state."}

  geom_line(

  ) +
  geom_point(

    size = 0.65,

  ) +

    linewidth = 0.45
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "#355C7D", "#5A9A9C", "#8A9B55",
      "#D39A45", "#AD5148"
    )[seq_len(best_pre1975_k)]
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 1960, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```
The three estimated state means range from
$-0.451\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $0.113\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
The lower-mean states mainly describe the earlier decades,
while the highest-mean state becomes more prominent from
the 1930s onward. The decoded path also returns to lower states,
rather than following a strictly increasing sequence.

Without the recent high-anomaly observations, a three-state
level model provides a more compact description under BIC.
However, the earlier sample still exhibits changes over time:
the reduced number of states does not establish stationarity
or confirm the existence of discrete physical regimes.
The transition matrix below reports the estimated monthly
probabilities for the shorter sample, with states ordered
by increasing mean anomaly.

```{r pre1975-transition-matrix}
pre1975_transition_raw <- t(vapply(
  seq_len(best_pre1975_k),
  function(j) {
    as.numeric(
      predict(best_pre1975_fit@transition[[j]])
    )
  },
  numeric(best_pre1975_k)
))

pre1975_transition <- pre1975_transition_raw[
  pre1975_order,
  pre1975_order,
  drop = FALSE
]

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(pre1975_transition)),
  all(pre1975_transition >= -1e-8),
  all(pre1975_transition <= 1 + 1e-8),
  all(abs(rowSums(pre1975_transition) - 1) < 1e-8)
)

pre1975_transition_table <- data.frame(
  From = paste("State", seq_len(best_pre1975_k)),
  pre1975_transition,
  check.names = FALSE
)

names(pre1975_transition_table)[-1] <- paste(
  "State", seq_len(best_pre1975_k)
)
```

```{r pre1975-transition-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  pre1975_transition_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Estimated monthly transition probabilities up to 1975.",
  position = "H"
)
```
All three states exhibit persistence, with estimated monthly
self-transition probabilities ranging from
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(diag(pre1975_transition)))` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(diag(pre1975_transition)))`.
Unlike the full-sample model, no state has an estimated
self-transition probability at the boundary value of one.
However, these probabilities are comparable to those of
the three lowest-mean states in the full-sample model.

Transitions mainly connect adjacent mean levels, allowing
movement toward both higher and lower anomalies. Persistence
alone does not establish that the states represent distinct,
long-lasting physical climate regimes.

# State-Dependent Linear Trend Model

To allow temperature anomalies to change within each state,
we replace the constant state means with linear functions of time:

\[
Y_t \mid S_t=j \sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(\alpha_j+\beta_j(t-1950),\sigma_j^2\right).
\]

Here, \(t\) is calendar time in years, \(\alpha_j\) is the
state-specific expected anomaly at 1950, and \(\beta_j\) is
the slope in degrees Celsius per year.

Transition probabilities remain constant over time.
The model does not impose continuity between state-specific
lines, so the decoded conditional mean may jump when states change.

We fit two- to five-state specifications to the full seasonally
adjusted sample and retain the model with the lowest BIC.

Each candidate model is estimated from 150 reproducible random
initializations. We retain the fit with the highest finite
log-likelihood and inspect its convergence status. A global
likelihood maximum is not guaranteed.
```{r fit-trend-models, results='hide', cache=TRUE}
climate_data$TimeCentered <- climate_data$Time - 1950

trend_seeds <- 123:272

trend_runs <- lapply(candidate_states, function(k) {
  fit_multiple_starts(
    response = Temperature ~ TimeCentered,
    data = climate_data,
    k = k,
    seeds = trend_seeds
  )
})

names(trend_runs) <- as.character(candidate_states)

trend_models <- lapply(trend_runs, function(x) x$model)

trend_comparison <- data.frame(
  States = candidate_states,
  LogLik = vapply(
    trend_models,
    function(model) as.numeric(logLik(model)),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  AIC = vapply(trend_models, AIC, numeric(1)),
  BIC = vapply(trend_models, BIC, numeric(1))
)

rownames(trend_comparison) <- NULL

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(trend_comparison$LogLik)),
  all(is.finite(trend_comparison$AIC)),
  all(is.finite(trend_comparison$BIC))
)

best_trend_k <- trend_comparison$States[
  which.min(trend_comparison$BIC)
]

best_trend_fit <- trend_models[[as.character(best_trend_k)]]
```

```{r trend-model-comparison, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  trend_comparison,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("States", "Log-likelihood", "AIC", "BIC"),
  caption = "Comparison of state-dependent linear trend models.",
  position = "H"
)
```
Both AIC and BIC favor the five-state trend model within the
candidate set. We therefore retain five states. Since this is
the largest specification considered, the comparison does not
establish whether additional states would further improve
the information criteria.

The selected trend model has a lower BIC than the selected
level model, by approximately
`r sprintf("%.1f", BIC(best_level_fit) - BIC(best_trend_fit))`
points. Both models use the same observations and seasonal
adjustment, so this comparison favors allowing within-state
linear trends among the specifications considered. It does
not establish that the decoded states correspond to physical
climate regimes.

States are ordered by increasing estimated slope. The intercept
represents the expected anomaly at 1950 under each state-specific
line; for states mainly occupied in other periods, this is an
extrapolated reference value.

The plotted conditional mean is calculated directly from the
estimated HMM coefficients along the Viterbi-decoded sequence.

```{r trend-state-parameters}
trend_parameters_raw <- t(vapply(
  seq_len(best_trend_k),
  function(j) {
    getpars(best_trend_fit@response[[j]][[1]])
  },
  numeric(3)
))

trend_order <- order(trend_parameters_raw[, 2])
trend_parameters <- trend_parameters_raw[
  trend_order,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

trend_mapping <- integer(best_trend_k)
trend_mapping[trend_order] <- seq_len(best_trend_k)

trend_states_raw <- posterior(best_trend_fit, type = "viterbi")$state
trend_states <- trend_mapping[trend_states_raw]

trend_decoded <- climate_data
trend_decoded$State <- factor(
  trend_states,
  levels = seq_len(best_trend_k)
)

trend_decoded$StateMean <-
  trend_parameters[trend_states, 1] +
  trend_parameters[trend_states, 2] *
  trend_decoded$TimeCentered

trend_state_table <- data.frame(
  State = seq_len(best_trend_k),
  Intercept = trend_parameters[, 1],
  Slope = trend_parameters[, 2],
  SD = trend_parameters[, 3],
  Months = tabulate(trend_states, nbins = best_trend_k)
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(trend_parameters)),
  all(trend_parameters[, 3] > 0),
  length(trend_states) == nrow(climate_data),
  sum(trend_state_table$Months) == nrow(climate_data),
  all(is.finite(trend_decoded$StateMean))
)
```

```{r trend-state-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  trend_state_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = c(0, 3, 4, 3, 0),
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "State", "Intercept (°C)", "Slope (°C/year)",
    "SD (°C)", "Decoded months"
  ),
  caption = "Estimated parameters and decoded occupancy of the trend model.",
  position = "H"
)
```

```{r trend-decoded-plot, fig.cap="Temperature anomalies colored by Viterbi-decoded state in the linear trend model. States are ordered by increasing slope. The black line follows the state-specific conditional mean along the decoded path."}
ggplot(trend_decoded, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Temperature),
    color = "grey75",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = Temperature, color = State),
    size = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = StateMean),
    color = "#222222",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "#355C7D", "#5A9A9C", "#D39A45",
      "#AD5148", "#8A9B55"
    )[seq_len(best_trend_k)]
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```
The estimated slopes range from
`r sprintf("%.4f", min(trend_state_table$Slope))` to
`r sprintf("%.4f", max(trend_state_table$Slope))` °C per year.
State 1 has a nearly flat fitted line. States 3 and 4 have
similar slopes but different intercepts, so they describe
different anomaly levels despite comparable rates of change.

The decoded path revisits states across different periods.
The highest-slope state appears during parts of the
1910s–1940s as well as in recent years. State labels therefore
do not represent a chronological sequence of successive
warming phases.

Allowing within-state trends captures gradual changes that
the level model represents through discrete shifts.
However, frequent switches between fitted lines still
produce jumps in the conditional mean. The decoded path
remains a descriptive approximation rather than evidence
of discrete physical climate regimes.

# Model Comparison

We compare the selected level and trend models with a two-state
trend specification as a simpler benchmark. All models in the
table use the same full sample and seasonal adjustment.

The model fitted up to 1975 is excluded from this information-criterion
comparison because it uses different observations.

```{r full-sample-model-comparison}
comparison_models <- list(
  "Selected level model" = best_level_fit,
  "Selected trend model" = best_trend_fit,
  "Two-state trend model" = trend_models[["2"]]
)

model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = names(comparison_models),
  States = c(best_level_k, best_trend_k, 2),
  Parameters = vapply(
    comparison_models,
    function(model) as.numeric(attr(logLik(model), "df")),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  LogLik = vapply(
    comparison_models,
    function(model) as.numeric(logLik(model)),
    numeric(1)
  ),
  AIC = vapply(comparison_models, AIC, numeric(1)),
  BIC = vapply(comparison_models, BIC, numeric(1))
)

rownames(model_comparison) <- NULL
```

```{r full-sample-comparison-table, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  model_comparison,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Model", "States", "Parameters",
    "Log-likelihood", "AIC", "BIC"
  ),
  caption = "Comparison of selected models and the two-state trend benchmark.",
  position = "H"
)
```
Among the three specifications reported here, the five-state
trend model has the lowest AIC and BIC. Its improvement in
fitted likelihood relative to the five-state level model
outweighs the penalty for its additional parameters.

The two-state trend benchmark has substantially higher
information criteria. Its simpler representation is therefore
less supported by this comparison. However, a two-state HMM
allows repeated switches between states: it should not be
interpreted as a model restricted to a single change point.

These comparisons concern in-sample fit penalized for model
complexity; they do not establish forecasting performance.

The decoded two-state benchmark illustrates how the simpler
specification represents the same observations. States are
ordered by increasing estimated slope, and the black line
follows the fitted conditional mean along the decoded sequence.

```{r two-state-trend-decoding}
two_state_fit <- trend_models[["2"]]

two_state_parameters_raw <- t(vapply(
  1:2,
  function(j) {
    getpars(two_state_fit@response[[j]][[1]])
  },
  numeric(3)
))

two_state_order <- order(two_state_parameters_raw[, 2])
two_state_parameters <- two_state_parameters_raw[
  two_state_order,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]

two_state_mapping <- integer(2)
two_state_mapping[two_state_order] <- 1:2

two_state_raw <- posterior(two_state_fit, type = "viterbi")$state
two_state_states <- two_state_mapping[two_state_raw]

two_state_decoded <- climate_data
two_state_decoded$State <- factor(
  two_state_states,
  levels = 1:2
)

two_state_decoded$StateMean <-
  two_state_parameters[two_state_states, 1] +
  two_state_parameters[two_state_states, 2] *
  two_state_decoded$TimeCentered

stopifnot(
  length(two_state_states) == nrow(climate_data),
  all(is.finite(two_state_parameters)),
  all(two_state_parameters[, 3] > 0),
  all(is.finite(two_state_decoded$StateMean))
)
```

```{r two-state-trend-plot, fig.cap="Two-state linear trend benchmark: seasonally adjusted anomalies colored by Viterbi-decoded state. The black line follows the estimated conditional mean. State labels are specific to this model."}
ggplot(two_state_decoded, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Temperature),
    color = "grey75",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = Temperature, color = State),
    size = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = StateMean),
    color = "#222222",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#355C7D", "#AD5148")
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    color = "State"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```
The two-state model captures the broad increase in anomalies,
but the decoded mean switches repeatedly between its two fitted
lines, particularly during the 1980s and 1990s. This illustrates
how a small number of state-specific trends can produce abrupt
changes in the fitted path despite gradual movements in the data.

We summarize switching frequency and spell lengths in the decoded
paths. We also examine lag-one autocorrelation of deviations from
the decoded state-specific means. These are descriptive diagnostics:
decoded states are estimated from the same observations.

```{r decoded-path-diagnostics}
summarize_path <- function(label, states, observed, fitted_mean) {
  spells <- rle(as.integer(states))
  residuals <- observed - fitted_mean

  data.frame(
    Model = label,
    Switches = length(spells$lengths) - 1L,
    MedianSpell = median(spells$lengths),
    ResidualACF = as.numeric(
      acf(residuals, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
    )
  )
}

path_diagnostics <- rbind(
  summarize_path(
    "Full-sample level",
    level_states,
    level_decoded$Temperature,
    level_decoded$StateMean
  ),
  summarize_path(
    "Level up to 1975",
    pre1975_states,
    pre1975_decoded$Temperature,
    pre1975_decoded$StateMean
  ),
  summarize_path(
    "Selected trend",
    trend_states,
    trend_decoded$Temperature,
    trend_decoded$StateMean
  ),
  summarize_path(
    "Two-state trend",
    two_state_states,
    two_state_decoded$Temperature,
    two_state_decoded$StateMean
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  path_diagnostics,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = c(0, 0, 1, 2),
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Model", "State switches",
    "Median spell (months)", "Residual ACF(1)"
  ),
  caption = "Decoded-path persistence and residual autocorrelation.",
  position = "H"
)
```
The selected five-state trend model produces 178 decoded
state switches, with a median spell length of seven months,
compared with 86 switches and eleven months for the full-sample
level model. Its improved information criteria therefore
accompany a more fragmented decoded path, rather than a
partition into a few sustained climate phases. The sample
ending in 1975 also exhibits frequent switching.

Lag-one residual autocorrelation remains positive in all
specifications. It is lower for the selected trend model
(0.15) than for the full-sample level model (0.39) and the
two-state trend benchmark (0.55). These descriptive diagnostics
suggest remaining serial structure, but do not constitute a
formal test of conditional independence or establish overfitting.

# Discussion and Limitations

Gaussian Hidden Markov Models provide a descriptive representation
of temperature anomalies through latent states. BIC selects five
states for the full-sample level model and three for the sample
ending in 1975. Allowing state-specific linear trends improves
the full-sample information criteria, with both AIC and BIC
favoring five states within the candidate set.

The results depend on the observation model. Constant state means
approximate gradual warming through changes of level, while
state-dependent trends allow movement within states but still
permit discontinuities when states change. The selected trend
model produces more frequent decoded switches and shorter median
spells than the level model. Improved information criteria therefore
do not imply a clearer partition into sustained climate regimes.

The specifications assume Gaussian observations, conditional
independence given the states, and constant transition probabilities.
Positive lag-one autocorrelation remains in deviations from the
decoded conditional means, suggesting residual serial structure.
This diagnostic does not constitute a formal test of conditional
independence. Additional states may partly accommodate dependence
or gradual change rather than identify distinct physical regimes.

Model selection is restricted to two through five states.
Estimation uses 25 random initializations per candidate for the
level models and 150 for the trend models. Multiple starts reduce
sensitivity to initialization but do not guarantee a global
likelihood maximum. Both selected full-sample models lie at the
upper end of the candidate range. Boundary transition estimates
also limit interpretation of state persistence.

Uncertainty in seasonal adjustment, parameter estimates, and
state assignments is not propagated into the reported results.
Estimation and decoding are retrospective: the analysis does
not establish physical change points, real-time state
identification, or out-of-sample forecasting performance.
